source_text: Satis mihi quidem videor probasse de falsa et vera divinitate, cum demonstravi, quemadmodum probatio consistat, non modo disputationibus nec argumentationibus, sed ipsorum etiam testimoniis, quos deos creditis, ut nihil jam ad hanc caussam sit retractandum. Quoniam tamen Romani nominis proprie mentio occurrit, non omittam congressionem, quam provocat illa praesumptio dicentium Romanos pro merito religiositatis diligentissimae in tantum sublimitatis elatos, ut orbem occuparint, et adeo deos esse, ut praeter caeteros floreant, qui illis officium praeter caeteros faciant. Scilicet ista merces Romanis a diis pro gratia expensa est, Sterculius, et Mutunus, et Larentina provexit imperium. Peregrinos enim deos non putem extraneae genti magis fautum voluisse quam suae, et patrium solum, in quo nati, adulti, nobilitati, sepultique sunt, transfretanis dedisse. Viderit Cybele, si urbem romanam ut memoriam Trojani generis adamavit, vernaculi sui scilicet adversus Achivorum arma protecti, si ad ultores transire prospexit, quos sciebat Graeciam Phrygiae debellatricem subacturos. Itaque majestatis suae in urbem collatae grande documentum nostrae etiam aetati proposuit, cum Marco Aurelio apud Sirmium reipublicae exempto, die decimo sexto Kalendarum Aprilium, Archigallus ille sanctissimus, die nono Kalend. earumdem, quo sanguinem impurum, lacertos quoque castrando libabat, pro salute imperatoris Marci jam intercepti solita aeque imperia mandavit. O nuntios tardos, o somniculosa diplomata, quorum vitio excessum imperatoris non ante Cybele cognovit, ne deam talem riderent Christiani. Sed non statim et Jupiter Cretam suam Romanis fascibus concuti sineret, oblitus antrum illud Idaeum, et aera Corybantia, et jucundissimum illic nutricis suae odorem. Nonne omni Capitolio tumulum illum suum praeposuisset, ut ea potius orbi terra praecelleret, quae cineres Jovis texit? Vellet Juno Punicam urbem posthabita Samo dilectam ab Aeneadarum utique genere deleri? Quod si Hic illius arma, Hic currus fuit, hoc regnum dea gentibus esse, Si qua fata sinant, jam tum tenditque fovetque. Misera illa conjux Jovis et soror adversus fata non valuit plane: Fato stat Jupiter ipse. Nec tantum tamen honoris Romani dicaverunt fatis dedentibus sibi Carthaginem adversus destinatum votumque Junonis, quantum prostitutissimae lupae Larentinae. Plures deos vestros regnasse certum est. Igitur si conferendi imperii tenent potestatem, cum ipsi regnarent, a quibus acceperant eam gratiam? quem coluerat Saturnus et Jupiter? aliquem opinor Sterculium [sed Romae postea], cum indigenis suis. Etiam si qui non regnarunt, tamen regnabatur ab aliis nondum cultoribus suis, ut qui nondum dii habebantur. Ergo aliorum est regnum dare, quia regnabatur multo ante quam isti dii inciderentur. Sed quam vanum est fastigium Romani nominis religiositatis meritis deputare, cum post imperium sive adhuc regnum [auctis jam rebus] religio profecerit. Nam etsi a Numa concepta est curiositas superstitiosa, nondum tamen aut simulacris aut templis res divina apud Romanos constabat; frugi religio et pauperes ritus, et nulla capitolia certantia coelo, sed temeraria de cespite altaria, et vasa adhuc Samia, et nidor ex illis, et Deus ipse nusquam. Nondum enim tunc ingenia Graecorum atque Tuscorum fingendis simulacris urbem inundaverant. Ergo non ante religiosi Romani, quam magni; ideoque non ob hoc magni, quia religiosi. Atqui quomodo ob religionem magni, quibus magnitudo de irreligiositate provenit? Ni fallor enim, omne regnum vel imperium bellis quaeritur et victoriis propagatur. Porro bella et victoriae captis et eversis plurimum urbibus constant. Id negotium sine deorum injuria non est. Eaedem strages moenium et templorum, pares caedes civium et sacerdotum, nec dissimiles rapinae sacrarum divitiarum et profanarum. Tot igitur sacrilegia Romanorum, quot trophaea; tot de diis, quot de gentibus triumphi; tot manubiae, quot manent adhuc simulacra captivorum deorum. Et ab hostibus ergo suis sustinent adorari, et illis imperium sine fine decernunt, quorum magis injurias quam adulationes remunerasse debuerant. Sed qui nihil sentiunt, tam impune laeduntur, quam frustra coluntur. Certe non potest fidei convenire, ut religionis meritis excrevisse videantur, qui, ut suggessimus, religionem aut laedendo creverunt, aut crescendo laeserunt. Etiam illi, quorum regna conflata sunt in imperii Romani summam, cum ea amitterent, sine religionibus non fuerunt.
pass_a_gloss: It seems to me that I have sufficiently proven about false and true divinity, when I demonstrated how the proof consists, not only in disputes and arguments, but also in the testimonies of those whom you consider gods, so that nothing is now to be withdrawn from this cause. Although the mention of the Roman name properly occurs, I will not omit the confrontation, which that presumption provokes, saying that the Romans, for the merit of diligent religiosity, have been elevated to such sublimity that they have occupied the world, and that they are gods, so that, beyond the others, they flourish, who perform a service beyond the others to them. Certainly, this reward has been expended by the gods to the Romans for gratitude, Sterculius, and Mutunus, and Larentina have advanced the empire. For I do not think that foreign gods have wished to favor a foreign nation more than their own, and that they have given the native soil, in which they were born, grown, ennobled, and buried, to those who cross over. Cybele will see if she has loved the Roman city as a memory of the Trojan race, certainly her own people, protected against the arms of the Achaeans, if she has looked to the avengers, whom she knew would subdue Greece, the conqueror of Phrygia. And so, a great document of her majesty, bestowed upon the city, has been proposed to our age as well, when, with Marcus Aurelius, the republic was exempt at Sirmium, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, that most holy Archigallus, on the ninth day before the Kalends of the same month, on which he was offering impure blood, and also castrating, ordered the usual commands for the salvation of Emperor Marcus, already intercepted. O slow messengers, o sleepy diplomas, whose fault it was that Cybele did not know of the emperor's death before, lest Christians ridicule such a goddess. But Jupiter would not immediately allow his Cretan land to be shaken by the Roman rods, having forgotten that Idaean cave, and the Corybantic bronze, and the most pleasant odor of his nurse there. Would he not have preferred that tomb of his to the whole Capitol, so that the earth might rather excel in the ashes that cover Jupiter? Would Juno have wished the Punic city, having put aside Samos, to be destroyed, loved by the race of the Aeneadae? What if this were the armor, this the chariot of that goddess, this the kingdom of the goddess among the nations, if the fates allow, already then she was striving and fostering. That wretched wife of Jupiter and sister was not able to prevail against the fates: Jupiter himself is established by fate. Nor have the fates, yielding to themselves, devoted as much honor to the Roman name as to the most prostituted she-wolf Larentina, against the destined vow and will of Juno. It is certain that many of your gods have reigned. Therefore, if they hold the power of conferring empire, from whom did they receive that grace, when they themselves reigned? Whom did Saturnus and Jupiter worship? Some, I think, Sterculius, but later in Rome, with their own indigenous people. Even if some did not reign, nevertheless, they were ruled by others, not yet their worshipers, so that they were not yet considered gods. Therefore, it is the kingdom of others to give, because the kingdom was ruled much before these gods were encountered. But how vain is the height of the Roman name to be attributed to the merits of religiosity, when, after the empire, or even the kingdom, religion has progressed. For even if the curiosity of superstition was conceived by Numa, nevertheless, the divine thing was not yet established among the Romans, either by statues or by temples; the religion was frugal, and the rites were poor, and there were no capitolias competing with the sky, but reckless altars from turf, and Samian vessels, and the smell from them, and God himself was nowhere. For the ingenuity of the Greeks and the Tuscans had not yet flooded the city with fabricated statues. Therefore, the Romans were not religious before they were great; and therefore, they were not great because they were religious. But how can they be great because of religion, when their greatness comes from irreligiosity? For, if I am not mistaken, every kingdom or empire is sought and propagated by wars and victories. Furthermore, wars and victories consist of the capture and destruction of many cities. This business is not without the injury of the gods. The same massacres of walls and temples, the same killings of citizens and priests, and the same plundering of sacred and profane riches. So many sacrileges of the Romans, so many trophies; so many triumphs over the gods, as over the nations; so many spoils, as many statues of captured gods still remain. And they are worshiped by their enemies, and they decree empire without end to those whose injuries they ought to have avenged rather than their flattery. But those who feel nothing are injured as impunity, as they are worshiped in vain. Certainly, it cannot be consistent with faith that they seem to have grown by the merits of religion, who, as we have suggested, have either increased their religion by injuring, or have injured by increasing. Even those whose kingdoms have been gathered into the sum of the Roman empire, when they lost them, were not without religions.

lemmas.gloss: Jupiter, the Roman king of the gods

pass_b_english: I have, I think, sufficiently proven the distinction between false and true divinity by showing that the proof rests not merely on debates and arguments, but also on the testimonies of the very beings you call gods, so that nothing further remains to be retracted on this point. Yet since the Roman name has been formally invoked, I will not pass over the challenge raised by the presumption that the Romans were elevated to such heights of world domination as a reward for their diligent religiosity — indeed, that they have become gods themselves, flourishing beyond all others because they render those others a service beyond all others. A fine reward the gods have paid the Romans for their gratitude: Sterculius, Mutunus, and Larentina advanced the empire. I hardly think foreign gods chose to favor a foreign nation over their own, handing over the native soil where they were born, grew up, were ennobled, and buried to men who crossed the sea. Let Cybele judge whether she loved the Roman city as a memorial of the Trojan race — her own people, shielded against the arms of the Achaeans — if she looked to the avengers she knew would subdue Greece, the conqueror of Phrygia. And so she has offered our own age a grand testament of her majesty bestowed upon the city: when Marcus Aurelius was away from the capital at Sirmium, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, that most holy Archigallus, on the ninth day before those same Kalends — the very day he was offering impure blood and even castrating himself — issued the usual orders for the salvation of the Emperor Marcus, already dead. O slow messengers, o sleepy dispatches, whose fault it was that Cybele did not learn of the emperor's death beforehand, lest Christians ridicule such a goddess. But Jupiter would not immediately allow his Cretan land to be shaken by the Roman rods, forgetting that Idaean cave, the Corybantic bronze, and the most pleasant odor of his nurse there. Would he not have preferred that tomb of his to the whole Capitol, so that the earth might rather excel in the ashes that cover Jupiter? Would Juno have wished the Punic city, setting aside Samos, to be destroyed — the city beloved by the race of the Aeneadae? What if these were her arms, this her chariot, this the kingdom of the goddess among the nations — if the fates allow, even then she was striving and fostering it. That wretched wife and sister of Jupiter could not prevail against the fates: Jupiter himself is established by fate. Nor did the fates, yielding to themselves, devote as much honor to the Roman name as to the most prostituted she-wolf Larentina, against the destined vow and will of Juno. It is certain that many of your gods have reigned. Therefore, if they hold the power of conferring empire, from whom did they receive that grace when they themselves reigned? Whom did Saturn and Jupiter worship? Some Sterculius, I think — but later in Rome, with their own indigenous people. Even if some did not reign, they were still ruled by others who were not yet their worshipers, so that they were not yet considered gods. It is therefore the province of others to give the kingdom, because the kingdom was ruled long before these gods were encountered. But how vain to attribute the heights of the Roman name to the merits of religiosity, when religion progressed only after the empire — or even the kingdom — had grown. For even if the curiosity of superstition was conceived by Numa, the divine was still not established among the Romans either by statues or by temples; religion was frugal, rites were poor, there were no Capitols competing with the sky, only reckless altars of turf, Samian vessels, the smell from them, and God himself was nowhere. For the ingenuity of the Greeks and Tuscans had not yet flooded the city with fabricated statues. Therefore the Romans were not religious before they were great; and so they were not great because they were religious. But how can they be great because of religion when their greatness springs from irreligion? For, if I am not mistaken, every kingdom or empire is sought by wars and propagated by victories. And wars and victories consist in the capture and destruction of countless cities. This business is not without injury to the gods: the same massacres of walls and temples, the same slaughter of citizens and priests, the same plundering of sacred and profane wealth. So many Roman sacrileges, so many trophies; so many triumphs over gods as over nations; so many spoils, as many statues of captured gods still remain. And they are worshiped by their enemies, and they decree endless empire to those whose injuries they ought to have avenged rather than flattered. But those who feel nothing are injured as impunely as they are worshiped in vain. It certainly cannot be consistent with faith that they appear to have grown by the merits of religion, when, as we have suggested, they either increased religion by injuring it, or injured it by increasing. Even those whose kingdoms were gathered into the sum of the Roman empire, when they lost them, were not without religions of their own.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex arguments regarding the relationship between Roman expansion and the development of their religion. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. All nuances regarding the Archigallus, the specific dates, and the theological paradoxes (increasing religion by injuring it) are preserved.
